front: What are the three main objectives of fiscal policy?
back:
1. Influence aggregate demand and growth (stabilisation)
2. Redistribute income and wealth
3. Allocate resources to public goods and services under-provided by markets
Multiplier = 1 / (1 - c(1 - t)), where c = marginal propensity to consume and t = income tax rate. Example: c = 0.8, t = 25% gives 1 / (1 - 0.6) = 2.5.

front: Why is a lump-sum tax cut less powerful than an equal spending increase?
back: Only the fraction c of the tax cut is spent in the first round (the rest is saved), so the output effect is c x multiplier x change in tax, versus multiplier x change in spending for government spending.

front: Automatic stabilisers vs discretionary fiscal policy
back: Automatic stabilisers (progressive taxes, unemployment benefits) change the budget counter-cyclically with no new decision and no lag. Discretionary policy needs new legislation and suffers lags.
Δ(D/Y) ≈ (r - g) x (D/Y) + primary deficit/GDP. The ratio rises if r > g with a primary deficit, and can fall if growth exceeds the real interest rate.

Rational households expect debt-financed tax cuts to be repaid by future taxes, so they save the tax cut. Private saving offsets public dissaving and deficits do not change aggregate demand. Requires strict assumptions.
Government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment. It is strongest at full employment and weak when there is spare capacity and low interest rates.

front: Name the three fiscal policy lags.
back: Recognition lag (seeing that the economy has turned), action lag (enacting the policy), impact lag (time for the policy to affect the economy).

A cyclical deficit arises from a weak economy (automatic stabilisers). A structural (cyclically adjusted) deficit would persist at full employment. Only structural changes show the discretionary stance.

front: Expansionary fiscal + contractionary monetary policy mix
back: Interest rates rise sharply, private spending falls, public spending rises. Effect on aggregate demand is ambiguous.
